chapter.title: Running it every day without you

cards.body:
What does your agent do on the morning you oversleep? If it's built right, the same as every other morning. The clipping service doesn't wait for your call: the person turns up at 7, reads the 5 papers and leaves the note on your desk, whether you're in the room or not.

Today the alarm clock goes in, and you choose the desk. **A schedule starts it, not you.**
cards.simpler: What does your agent do on a morning you sleep in? If it is built well, the same thing it does every morning. Think of a clipping service. The person arrives at 7, reads the 5 papers and leaves a note on your desk, whether you are there or not. Today you add the alarm clock and pick the desk. **A schedule starts it, not you.**

cards.prompt: Your agent can fetch, compare and summarise. Every morning you open a terminal and type the command that runs it. Then you spend a week on holiday in Lisbon with no laptop. What does your agent catch that week?

options.text: Everything. It saves the changes up for when you get back.
Only the big changes, like price rises.

whyNot.a: That's the saved copy from chapter 3, not the trigger: copies only get made when something runs the agent.
whyNot.c: That's the model judging what matters, not the trigger: if nothing runs, nothing gets judged.

cards.reteach: The clipping service only works if someone shows up. A script waits for you to start it. An agent has an alarm clock that starts it, so with no alarm you get no clippings, however clever the rest is.

cards.title: The alarm clock
cards.body:
A *schedule* is a rule like "every day at 7:00, run this." On Linux, and usually on Macs too, a simple alarm clock is *cron*: one short line, and it runs your program on time.

The line looks like a bus timetable in shorthand: "0 7 * * *". Left to right that's minute 0, hour 7, any day of the month, any month, any weekday. **Five slots, one time, every day.**

The catch is that cron lives on one machine. If your laptop is shut at 7:00, the alarm goes off in an empty room and nothing runs. That's why many people run their agent on a rented computer that never sleeps, called a *server*.
cards.simpler: A schedule is a rule like "every day at 7:00, run this." A simple alarm clock on Linux, and usually on Macs too, is cron. It reads one short line, like "0 7 * * *", and runs your program then. That means minute 0, hour 7, any day, any month, any weekday. **Five slots, one time, every day.** But cron lives on one computer. If your laptop is shut at 7:00, nothing runs. So many people use a server, a rented computer that never sleeps.

cards.title: Tuesday, 7:02
cards.body: Dana watches 4 rivals. Dana's cron line is "0 7 * * *", and it runs fetch, compare and summarise in that order. On Tuesday at 7:02 a chat message lands on Dana's phone: "Acme: Pro plan now $35 a month, was $29. Source: Acme pricing page, line 14." Dana reads it in the coffee queue. Acme's own help pages still say $29, so Dana spotted it before Acme had even updated its own help pages.
cards.simpler: Dana keeps an eye on 4 rivals. Dana's cron line is "0 7 * * *", and it runs three steps in order: fetch, compare, summarise. On Tuesday at 7:02, a chat message reaches Dana's phone: "Acme: Pro plan now $35 a month, was $29. Source: Acme pricing page, line 14." Dana reads it in the coffee queue. Acme's own help pages still say $29, so **Dana spotted it before Acme had even updated its own help pages.**

cards.prompt: Jo's agent works when Jo runs it by hand. Jo wants the summary by 8:00 every morning, before the team meeting. Which setup gets it there?

options.text: The cron line "30 7 * * *" on a server that stays on, sending Jo a chat message.
The same cron line on Jo's laptop, which sleeps in a bag overnight.
A sticky note on Jo's screen: "run the agent at 7:30".

whyNot.b: That's the right alarm in the wrong room: on a sleeping laptop, cron never goes off.
whyNot.c: That's Jo acting as the trigger, not a schedule: it's still a script Jo has to start by hand.

cards.reteach: Two things have to be true at 7:30: the alarm is set, and the machine it's set on is awake. Only a computer that stays on can keep an appointment you slept through.

cards.title: The desk
cards.body:
You'd think the schedule is the hard part. It isn't. The desk is. A note left in a drawer you never open is the same as no note.

**Send the summary to a place you already check before 9am**: your inbox, a chat app on your phone, a channel your team reads. A file on disk is fine while you're testing. After that it's a dusty attic.

One more thing about clocks. Rented servers often run on *UTC*, the world's reference time. "7:00" there is 3:00 in New York in summer. Check which clock your alarm is reading.
cards.simpler: The hard part isn't the schedule. It's the desk. A note in a drawer you never open is the same as no note. **Send the summary to a place you already check before 9am**: your inbox, a chat app on your phone, or a channel your team reads. A file is fine while testing, then it just gathers dust. Rented servers often use UTC, the world's reference clock. 7:00 there is 3:00 in New York in summer, so check which clock yours reads.

cards.body: Sam set the agent to write each summary to a file called notes.txt in a folder named agent. It ran perfectly for 3 weeks. Sam found the folder on day 22, holding 21 unread notes and a rival's price cut that was already old news. **If you can't remember the last summary you read, the desk is in the wrong room.**
cards.simpler: Sam had the agent write each summary to a file called notes.txt in a folder named agent. It worked perfectly for 3 weeks. On day 22, Sam finally opened the folder. Inside were 21 unread notes, plus news of a rival's price cut that was already old. **If you can't remember the last summary you read, the desk is in the wrong room.**

cards.prompt: Which pair turns your fetch-compare-summarise script into something that runs without you?

options.text: A smarter model and a longer list of pages.
A schedule on a machine that stays awake, plus delivery to a place you already check.
A saved copy of each page and a line-by-line comparison.

whyNot.a: That's chapters 2 and 5, not running on its own: reading more doesn't make the agent start itself.
whyNot.c: That's the clippings and the scissors from chapters 3 and 4, not the alarm clock and the desk.

cards.reteach: Picture the clipping service again. The reading and cutting already work. What's missing is someone who turns up at 7 without being called, and a desk you actually sit at.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: A script becomes an agent when a schedule starts it instead of you: a cron line like "0 7 * * *" on a machine that stays awake. And the summary only counts if it lands where you already look every morning.
cards.simpler: A script turns into an agent when **a schedule starts it instead of you**. That means a cron line like "0 7 * * *" on a computer that stays awake. And the summary only counts if it lands where you already look every morning.

cards.body:
Write down the one place you check before 9am every day: inbox, chat app, something else. That's your agent's desk. On a Mac, type crontab -l in Terminal to see any cron alarms already set.

Tomorrow: your agent will be wrong within a week. Three checks catch it in 2 minutes.
cards.simpler: Write down the one place you check before 9am every day, like your inbox, a chat app, or something else. **That place is your agent's desk**, where its summary will land. On a Mac, open Terminal and type crontab -l to see any cron alarms that are already set. Tomorrow: your agent will be wrong within a week, and three checks catch it in 2 minutes.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now set your agent to run once a day on its own and send its summary somewhere you'll actually see it.

dubious_claims: 'so Dana knew before Acme's support team did' does not follow: outdated help pages don't show the support team didn't know about the price change
'the oldest alarm clock is cron' on Mac is misleading: macOS now prefers launchd, its own built-in scheduler, and cron may need Full Disk Access to reach some folders
repairedFrom.why: Card 3 is about 121 words, counting each * in the cron line as a word, so it goes over the limit. It also does three jobs at once: it explains what a schedule is, how to read a cron line, and why you need a server. Two smaller problems are elsewhere: the desk idea is never tested on its own, and the chapter's last card is the 'try' card, so the 'Tomorrow' hook in card 9 isn't the closing line.
repairedFrom.fix: In card 3, replace 'On Mac and Linux the oldest alarm clock is *cron*, a tool built into the computer that reads one short line and runs your program at that time.' with 'On Mac and Linux that alarm clock is *cron*: one short line, and it runs your program on time.' That cuts about 15 words. Then move the 'Tomorrow: your agent will be wrong within a week…' line to the end of the try card.
